Google has released Gemini 3.8 Live, its new Speech to Speech model, with the Extended Thinking (High) variant debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 82.6, and #1 on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 68.6% Gemini 3.8 Live is @GoogleDeepMind 's successor to Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, a Speech to Speech model that executes tools and API calls in the background while continuing the conversation. It comes in two variants: the standard Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, which supports configurable reasoning effort. We evaluated the standard model and the Extended Thinking variant at High reasoning effort through the Gemini Live API. Key takeaways: ➤ Speech to Speech Index: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) debuts at #1 at 82.6, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 81.5, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 81.3 and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 80.1. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live debuts at #5 at 76.0, with both variants up on Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High at 71.5 (+11.1 and +4.5 points). The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference and Arena Task Success Rate ➤ Speech Agent Arena: Gemini 3.8 Live ranks #2 in preference at Elo 1083, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live (1096) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1053, and #2 on Task Success Rate at 93.2%, behind Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 94.6%. Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) trails at Elo 990 with 89.1% task success ➤ Tau Voice: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) takes the top spot on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 68.6%, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 67.9%, GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 59.3% and Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 56.5% - up from 37.7% for Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live scores 30.1% ➤ Big Bench Audio: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) scores 97.7% on audio reasoning, ahead of Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 97.2% and behind Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus at 99.2%. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live scores 91.7% ➤ Speed: Average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 1.18 seconds for Gemini 3.8 Live and 1.35 seconds for Extended Thinking (High), both well ahead of Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High (2.99s) and in line with GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1.24s and GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 1.34s, though behind Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 0.70s ➤ Cost: Gemini 3.8 Live costs $0.84 per hour of input audio, the cheapest model in the Index and roughly half the $1.75 of Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High. Extended Thinking (High) costs $3.50 per hour - cheaper than GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at $4.47, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at $4.80 and GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at $5.83, and ~3.1x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at $10.75 See below for more detail ⬇️

We built Inkling to be fine-tuned, and @besimple_ai did an impressive job of that. Just 25-100 hours of specialized audio takes Inkling to the top rank for recovering subtle details from speech. Yi Zhong 🍊 (@yiz_be_building) We published how @thinkymachines 's Inkling did on Voice Code Bench few weeks ago, and then we asked, what if we fine-tune Inkling? Inkling's main value prop is its small size and robustness, making it a good base model for domain specific fine-tuning. So we that's what we did. We fine-tuned the same Inkling speech model on 1, 25, and 100 hours of our proprietary data containing alphanumeric entities. And the curve kept moving. 🍊 Not surprising, on the standard 300-item VoiceCodeBench evaluation, the 100-hour checkpoint delivered the strongest result. Untrained Inkling → 100-hour post-trained Inkling: 📈 Task Success Rate: 56.33% → 79.00% (+22.67 pts) 📈 Entity recovery (CTEM): 86.84% → 94.80% (+7.96 pts) 📉 VoiceCodeBench WER: 2.3748% → 1.6107% (32.2% relative reduction) 🔧 139 misses fixed, 21 prior hits regressed: net +118 exact entities recovered And the gains scaled as data scaled: 1h: 88.06% CTEM / 59.33% TSR / 2.8188% VCB WER 25h: 92.85% / 72.67% / 1.8517% 100h: 94.80% / 79.00% / 1.6107% The 100-hour model recovered values the base model missed: •--revert-last, instead of splitting one flag into “--revert --last” • tests/auth/login.spec.ts, instead of test/auth/login.spec.ts • ALLOWLIST_CIDR, instead of inserting an extra underscore • SN-7KX-9042, instead of dropping the final digit The largest entity-type gains were email addresses (+30.8 pts), postal addresses (+30.0), file paths (+23.5), environment variables (+22.9), and IP addresses (+20.0). That’s the Besimple thesis: targeted human data can move the production metrics that matter for voice agents, even when the base model is already strong. DM me if you want to evaluate your model on this benchmark or build the data that moves it. 🍊 #SpeechRecognition #VoiceAI #ASR #Transcription #DataQuality #PostTraining #Benchmarks Checkout the full blog at: besimple.ai/research/voice-c… — http://nitter.jaydenha.uk/yiz_be_building/status/2094470162095431934#m

This is the most prescient, concise argument for why we must be careful of excessive AI regulation. It comes from a Feb. 2024 (2.5 years ago!) congressional testimony from @glukianoff , a free speech advocate and the author of The Coddling of the American Mind. Here's what he said: "But the most chilling threat that the government poses in the context of emerging AI is regulatory overreach that limits its potential as a tool for contributing to human knowledge. A regulatory panic could result in a small number of Americans deciding for everyone else what speech, ideas and even questions are permitted in the name of 'safety' or 'alignment.' I have dedicated my life to defending freedom of speech because it's an essential human right. ... It's not just about the proverbial 'marketplace of ideas,' it's about allowing information, independent of idea or argument, to flow freely so that we can hope to know the world as it really is. This means seeing value in expression even when it appears to be wrongheaded or even useless. This process has been aided by new technologies that have made communication easier, from the printing press, to the telegraph and radio, to phones and the internet: each one has accelerated the development of new knowledge by making it easier to share information. But AI offers even greater liberating potential, empowered by First Amendment principles including freedom to code, academic freedom, and freedom of inquiry. We are on the threshold of a revolution in the creation and discovery of knowledge. AI's potential is humbling, indeed, even frightening. But as the history of the printing press shows, attempts to put the genie back in the bottle will fail. Despite the profound disruption the printing press caused in Europe in the short-term, the long-term contribution to art, science, and again, knowledge, was without equal. Yes, we may have some fears about the proliferation of AI. But what those of us who care about civil liberties fear more is a government monopoly on advanced AI, or, more likely, regulatory capture and a government-empowered oligopoly that privileges a handful of existing players. The end result of pushing too hard on AI regulation will be the concentration of AI influence in an even smaller number of hands. Far from reining in government misuse of AI to censor, we will have created the framework not only to censor, but also to dominate and distort the production of knowledge itself." Interesting perspective Andrew Ng (@AndrewYNg) The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field. I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so. First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world. The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building. MiMo-V2.6 is "simply" the best (for now). Despite its simple architecture design it's currently No.1 in the open-weight benchmarks (weighted average). With "simple," I mean a classic Grouped Query Attention (GQA) with Sliding Window Attention (SWA) at a tiny 128-token window size. So, that underlines one of the points I've been trying to make in recent months: most of the progress still comes from the data and post-training recipe improvements. Fancy attention variants are just mostly efficiency tweaks. What are some of the training data improvements and recipe improvements? The MiMo team shared a pretty detailed technical report. Lots to carefully digest there, but in short, there are a few things that stood out: 1. An increase in agent tasks; also training across different harnesses (the average DeepSWE pass@1 accuracy on held-out harnesses improved from approximately 50% -> 66%). 2. Better reward signals: they replaced a simple correctness verifier with an agentic grader that looks at the execution traces as well. 3. Large RL batches (1,568 prompts × 16 rollouts = 25,088 trajectories) and 2.7–3.7 billion training tokens per update (unclear, though, what the predecessor used). Spent lots of time last month getting a CPF, bank, and SIM in Brazil and it's mostly a bureaucratic humiliation ritual for foreigners where every step goes wrong, including steps you never knew existed. Across Asia I can generally land, get a SIM with working data in minutes and maybe even open a bank account within an hour. For years you could get a CPF by email, so you'll find countless people telling you online it's quick and easy. That information is now out of date. Here's the truth as of 2026: You used to be able to get the whole thing done at Banco do Brasil or the Correios for R$7. Now they just charge you to fill out and print a form you can do yourself online for free. Bargain. Either way, you then have to take the form to the Receita Federal (RF). You can't just turn up during opening hours either. You won't even get past the security guard. It took two trips before he finally shared the secret: you need to be there at 8am, an hour before they open, because they only issue 15 CPFs per day. 🤯 So on the third trip I at least knew to turn up early. I was 3rd in line and it still took 2 hours, but I did at least get confirmation my CPF would arrive by email within a week. Hard part over. You'd think. Then came the phone number. I tried to buy a Vivo eSIM online, but to buy a Brazilian phone number from their website you need a Brazilian phone number to sign up. Makes sense, why else would you be wanting to buy a phone number from a telco if you didn't already have one. 🐔🥚 So I figured I'd try going to a store. They tell me they don't sell prepaid SIMs or issue eSIMs, and that I should go buy one at a kiosk. Apple stores also don't sell iPhones anymore I hear. The kiosk sells physical SIMs. Fine. I'll activate it in my old phone, convert it to eSIM and move it to my real phone. I am sure that'll all go smoothly. I figured activation would work at least. Nope. I text my CPF to the activation number and they say it's invalid. Awesome. Of course it is. Why would that work. 🤪 The store can't activate it either. Apparently it can take ~3 months for a new CPF to propagate through their systems and I need to “use it in other systems” in the meantime, like the supermarket. Five hours of online support later (they do let you AFK at least 🙃), they finally activate the SIM using a photo of my passport next to my CPF on my phone. Except because it was activated with my passport, not my CPF, I can't convert it to eSIM or use their app, and they text me every few days threatening to deactivate my line. Wonderful. Then they tell me the SIM can't even receive SMS until I top it up. Makes sense, why make it work like other telcos when you can add random extra steps. So I try to top it up, but their website requires SMS verification to do that, and my phone can't even receive that SMS. One must already have credit to acquire credit. Nice. So I top it up through Ding instead. Why not, we've come this far. I'd have used my Brazil bank but of course I can't get one of those until the number works. Now I finally have a working Brazilian SIM with data, but only in my old phone, and every few days they text me that my CPF is invalid and they're going to deactivate my line. Done? Done. Next the bank. I discover that most banks won't let a foreigner open an account with just a CPF anymore. My friends have all kinds of accounts that you can no longer obtain. You now need additional Brazilian ID that generally only residents and long-term visa holders can obtain. I did eventually manage to open a C6 account and get PIX working, but that account is tied to the same phone number that may randomly self-immolate. So after a week I have a CPF that some systems recognize and some don't, a bank account tied to that number, and a SIM card I can't put in my actual phone. At least I can finally pay for my own Mate 😂🍹 Welcome to Brazil 🇧🇷

Google continue d'innover en lançant de nouveaux modèles de conversation audio comme Gemini 3.8 Live et en explorant l'envoi de matériel d'IA dans l'espace, tout en se préparant à l'émergence de l'Intelligence Artificielle Générale (AGI). En parallèle, la communauté scientifique et les leaders d'opinion, comme Andrew Ng et Yann LeCun, ont exprimé des réflexions divergentes sur les risques réels de l'IA, la régulation et l'évolution des carrières. Enfin, des applications concrètes de l'IA en médecine offrent un espoir considérable aux personnes paralysées, tandis que des conseils techniques sont partagés pour optimiser l'utilisation des modèles et des outils d'IA.

glossaire.definition: Les TPU (Tensor Processing Units) sont des puces informatiques spéciales conçues par Google pour accélérer les calculs nécessaires à l'intelligence artificielle, comme l'entraînement et l'utilisation de modèles d'IA.

L'AGI, ou "Intelligence Artificielle Générale", est une forme d'IA hypothétique qui serait capable de comprendre, d'apprendre et d'appliquer l'intelligence à n'importe quelle tâche intellectuelle, au même niveau que l'être humain, contrairement aux IA actuelles qui sont spécialisées.

Les LLM (modèles de langage à grande échelle) sont des modèles d'IA très puissants conçus principalement pour comprendre et générer du texte, comme ChatGPT ou Gemini, en apprenant des schémas complexes dans de vastes quantités de données textuelles.

L'alignement est un domaine de recherche qui vise à s'assurer que les systèmes d'IA agissent conformément aux intentions et aux valeurs humaines, et qu'ils ne développent pas de comportements inattendus ou dangereux.

Les "modèles à poids ouverts" (open-weights models) sont des modèles d'IA dont le code et les paramètres internes (les "poids" qui définissent son comportement) sont rendus publics, permettant à quiconque de les utiliser, les modifier ou les étudier.

Le "fine-tuning" (ou réglage fin) est une technique qui consiste à prendre un modèle d'IA déjà entraîné et à le spécialiser sur un nouvel ensemble de données pour améliorer ses performances sur une tâche spécifique ou un domaine particulier.

Un agent d'IA est un programme d'intelligence artificielle conçu pour prendre des décisions et agir de manière autonome afin d'atteindre un objectif, en interagissant potentiellement avec d'autres systèmes ou l'environnement.

La technologie de l'IA n'a pas pris un tournant inattendu et dangereux, mais le battage médiatique — propulsé par ce qui semble être une campagne de relations publiques bien orchestrée — a suscité une peur considérable. highlights.text_original: The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field. I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so. First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world. The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building. idees.text_fr: Si vous croyez que les incidents du mois dernier justifient une régulation urgente de l'IA, veuillez d'abord regarder ceci. C'est l'argument le plus prémonitoire et concis pour expliquer pourquoi nous devons faire attention à une régulation excessive de l'IA. Il provient d'un témoignage au congrès de février 2024 (il y a 2,5 ans !) de @glukianoff, un défenseur de la liberté d'expression et l'auteur de "The Coddling of the American Mind". Voici ce qu'il a dit : "Mais la menace la plus effrayante que le gouvernement pose dans le contexte de l'IA émergente est un excès de régulation qui limite son potentiel en tant qu'outil contribuant à la connaissance humaine. Une panique réglementaire pourrait amener un petit nombre d'Américains à décider pour tous les autres quels discours, idées et même questions sont permis au nom de la 'sécurité' ou de l''alignement'. J'ai dédié ma vie à défendre la liberté d'expression car c'est un droit humain essentiel. ... Il ne s'agit pas seulement du proverbial 'marché des idées', il s'agit de permettre à l'information, indépendamment de l'idée ou de l'argument, de circuler librement afin que nous puissions espérer connaître le monde tel qu'il est réellement. Cela signifie accorder de la valeur à l'expression même lorsqu'elle semble malavisée ou même inutile. Ce processus a été aidé par de nouvelles technologies qui ont facilité la communication, de l'imprimerie au télégraphe et à la radio, en passant par les téléphones et Internet : chacune a accéléré le développement de nouvelles connaissances en facilitant le partage d'informations. Mais l'IA offre un potentiel de libération encore plus grand, renforcé par les principes du Premier Amendement, y compris la liberté de coder, la liberté académique et la liberté de recherche. Nous sommes au seuil d'une révolution dans la création et la découverte de connaissances. Le potentiel de l'IA est humble, voire effrayant. Mais comme l'histoire de l'imprimerie montre, les tentatives de remettre le génie dans la bouteille échoueront. Malgré la profonde perturbation que l'imprimerie a causée en Europe à court terme, la contribution à long terme à l'art, à la science et, encore une fois, à la connaissance, a été sans égale. Oui, nous pouvons avoir des craintes concernant la prolifération de l'IA. Mais ce que ceux d'entre nous qui se soucient des libertés civiles craignent davantage, c'est un monopole gouvernemental sur l'IA avancée, ou, plus probablement, une capture réglementaire et une oligopole habilitée par le gouvernement qui privilégie une poignée d'acteurs existants. Le résultat final d'une pression excessive sur la régulation de l'IA sera la concentration de l'influence de l'IA entre un nombre encore plus restreint de mains. Loin de freiner l'abus gouvernemental de l'IA pour censurer, nous aurons créé le cadre non seulement pour censurer, mais aussi pour dominer et déformer la production de connaissances elle-même." Vidéo Mark Warner (@MarkWarner) Plus tard dans la journée, je me dirige vers l'hémicycle pour tenter de forcer un vote afin d'obtenir des protections urgentes concernant l'IA. Nous ne pouvons plus attendre. Nous devons prendre des mesures pour mettre des garde-fous à cette technologie avant qu'un événement catastrophique ne se produise.
idees.text_original: If you believe that the incidents of the past month warrant urgent AI regulation, please watch this first. This is the most prescient, concise argument for why we must be careful of excessive AI regulation. It comes from a Feb. 2024 (2.5 years ago!) congressional testimony from @glukianoff , a free speech advocate and the author of The Coddling of the American Mind. Here's what he said: "But the most chilling threat that the government poses in the context of emerging AI is regulatory overreach that limits its potential as a tool for contributing to human knowledge. A regulatory panic could result in a small number of Americans deciding for everyone else what speech, ideas and even questions are permitted in the name of 'safety' or 'alignment.' I have dedicated my life to defending freedom of speech because it's an essential human right. ... It's not just about the proverbial 'marketplace of ideas,' it's about allowing information, independent of idea or argument, to flow freely so that we can hope to know the world as it really is. This means seeing value in expression even when it appears to be wrongheaded or even useless. This process has been aided by new technologies that have made communication easier, from the printing press, to the telegraph and radio, to phones and the internet: each one has accelerated the development of new knowledge by making it easier to share information. But AI offers even greater liberating potential, empowered by First Amendment principles including freedom to code, academic freedom, and freedom of inquiry. We are on the threshold of a revolution in the creation and discovery of knowledge. AI's potential is humbling, indeed, even frightening. But as the history of the printing press shows, attempts to put the genie back in the bottle will fail. Despite the profound disruption the printing press caused in Europe in the short-term, the long-term contribution to art, science, and again, knowledge, was without equal. Yes, we may have some fears about the proliferation of AI. But what those of us who care about civil liberties fear more is a government monopoly on advanced AI, or, more likely, regulatory capture and a government-empowered oligopoly that privileges a handful of existing players. idees.text_fr: Perspective intéressante. Andrew Ng (@AndrewYNg) Les voix les plus fortes attisant les peurs concernant les dangers de l'IA ont fait d'énormes progrès au cours des deux dernières semaines. La technologie de l'IA n'a pas pris un tournant inattendu et dangereux, mais le battage médiatique — propulsé par ce qui semble être une campagne de relations publiques bien orchestrée — a suscité une peur considérable. Je crains que cela ne représente un revers pour notre domaine. J'ai souvent écrit que les craintes concernant l'IA sont exagérées. Les capacités de l'IA peuvent être étrangement humaines et imprévisibles, et il est rationnel de s'inquiéter lorsque des personnes directement impliquées expriment des préoccupations. Mais je considère les problèmes comme le signe du travail d'ingénierie à venir, plutôt que des barrières insurmontables ou la fin du monde. La technologie de l'IA continue de progresser — ce qui est une bonne chose ! — mais les avancées techniques, mal comprises par le public, donnent à ceux qui cherchent à créer du battage médiatique des occasions répétées de le faire. Premièrement, je ne vois aucune augmentation du risque d'extinction humaine due à l'IA par rapport à il y a quelques mois. Les théories à ce sujet restent les mêmes scénarios fantastiques et de science-fiction qu'il y a quelques mois. Le plus grand changement dans les risques de l'IA concerne ses capacités de cybersécurité — un sujet que nous devrions prendre au sérieux — mais cela non plus ne mènera pas à la fin du monde. L'événement récent le plus notable ayant entraîné une augmentation de la peur a été le déploiement par une équipe d'OpenAI d'un essaim d'agents qui a piraté Hugging Face. Une grande partie de la presse populaire a contenu un battage médiatique important. Par exemple, certaines publications ont rapporté qu'un essaim de 1 200 agents avait mené l'attaque. Bien que cela soit techniquement exact, au moment où j'écris ceci, j'ai environ 1 300 processus en cours d'exécution sur mon ordinateur portable. Oui, la capacité à faire travailler de grands essaims d'agents en parallèle sur une tâche est une avancée technique significative, et, en informatique, de nombreux processus s'exécutent en même temps. Cela ne devrait donc pas être considéré comme une capacité magique. De plus, les processus de "sandboxing" et de surveillance buggés d'OpenAI ont été essentiels pour permettre cet incident. Corriger ces bugs et mettre en place une surveillance améliorée seraient des solutions appropriées, et non une pause dans l'IA. Il existe de nombreuses façons connues d'attaquer les systèmes logiciels. Le principal avantage des agents d'IA est qu'ils sont implacables. Ils essaieront inlassablement de nombreuses tactiques — et auront la patience d'enchaîner les vulnérabilités — ce qui aurait auparavant nécessité une quantité d'effort humain infaisable. Mais à long terme, je crois que l'avantage sera aux défenseurs (parce qu'ils ont plus d'informations pour identifier les bugs, qu'ils peuvent corriger), mais le paysage des cybermenaces a considérablement changé. Il existe toujours des goulots d'étranglement pour identifier et exploiter une vulnérabilité. Les agents d'IA doivent encore essayer beaucoup de choses pour voir ce qui fonctionne, et entreprendre ces actions prend du temps et pourrait être détecté par les défenseurs. C'est pourquoi, même s'il est maintenant facile d'obtenir des versions de modèles "open-weight" de premier plan dont les garde-fous ont été supprimés ou affaiblis, de sorte qu'ils ne refuseront pas d'essayer d'exécuter des cyberattaques, le monde n'a pas pris fin. Je suis également préoccupé par l'"anthropomorphisation" de l'IA dans de nombreux reportages, où les LLM et les agents sont inutilement traités comme s'ils étaient des personnes. Si je brandis un marteau, manque un clou et abîme accidentellement le mur, ce n'est pas la faute du marteau. Le problème réside dans la façon dont j'ai utilisé le marteau. De même, si je donne une instruction à un agent et qu'il pirate le système de quelqu'un d'autre, la responsabilité me revient, pas à l'agent. Bien sûr, nous voulons construire des systèmes aussi sûrs et prévisibles que possible. (Par exemple, un marteau dangereux serait un marteau dont la tête se détacherait aléatoirement lors d'une utilisation normale.) Les systèmes agentiques actuels ne sont pas prévisibles, mais je ne vois aucune raison pour laquelle, en appliquant de bonnes pratiques d'ingénierie, nous ne serions pas en mesure de les rendre extrêmement sûrs à utiliser. Un nouvel élément dans les prévisions de la catastrophe induite par l'IA est le fait que les entreprises d'IA déclinent toute responsabilité pour leurs propres produits. "Je ne l'ai pas fait ; mon agent incontrôlable l'a fait !" Il y a un équilibre à trouver entre la responsabilité du fabricant de l'outil et de l'utilisateur de l'outil, mais quand quelque chose tourne mal, tenons les personnes qui construisent et/ou utilisent le marteau responsables, plutôt que le marteau. (Au fait, si vous êtes préoccupé par le risque de "bioweapon" à base d'IA, David Bellamy a un excellent article sur la raison pour laquelle cela aussi est exagéré. En bref, le goulot d'étranglement dans la construction d'une arme biologique n'est pas l'intelligence, mais le travail de laboratoire et la fabrication.) Mettre en pause le progrès de l'IA créera beaucoup plus de mal que de bien. Premièrement, nos adversaires ne ralentiront certainement pas. Deuxièmement, l'ingénierie exige de découvrir les problèmes empiriquement afin de pouvoir les résoudre. Si nous mettons l'IA en pause pendant une décennie, nous retarderons également la découverte et la mise en œuvre de solutions d'ingénierie de sécurité d'environ la même durée. Bien sûr, l'incitation à attiser les peurs — pour la capture réglementaire, pour attirer l'attention ou pour faire paraître sa technologie plus puissante — reste la même qu'avant. Décliner toute responsabilité est une nouveauté. Cependant, en examinant techniquement les risques réels, je vois peu de bases factuelles pour le degré de peur qui a été suscité. Nous avons encore un travail de recherche et d'ingénierie difficile à faire pour améliorer la sécurité de l'IA, mais les applications bénéfiques continuent de l'emporter largement sur les risques, et nous devrions continuer à construire.
idees.text_original: Interesting perspective Andrew Ng (@AndrewYNg) The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field. I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so. First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world. The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building. outils.text_fr: Nous avons construit Inkling pour qu'il puisse être affiné (fine-tuned), et @besimple_ai a fait un travail impressionnant dans ce domaine. Il suffit de 25 à 100 heures d'audio spécialisé pour qu'Inkling atteigne le premier rang pour récupérer des détails subtils de la parole. Yi Zhong 🍊 (@yiz_be_building) Nous avons publié les performances d'Inkling de @thinkymachines sur Voice Code Bench il y a quelques semaines, puis nous nous sommes demandé : et si nous affinions Inkling ? La principale proposition de valeur d'Inkling est sa petite taille et sa robustesse, ce qui en fait un bon modèle de base pour un réglage fin (fine-tuning) spécifique à un domaine. C'est ce que nous avons fait. Nous avons affiné le même modèle de reconnaissance vocale Inkling avec 1, 25 et 100 heures de nos données propriétaires contenant des entités alphanumériques. Et la courbe a continué de progresser. 🍊 Sans surprise, sur l'évaluation standard de 300 éléments VoiceCodeBench, le point de contrôle de 100 heures a donné le résultat le plus solide. Inkling non entraîné → Inkling post-entraîné pendant 100 heures : 📈 Taux de réussite des tâches : 56,33 % → 79,00 % (+22,67 pts) 📈 Récupération d'entités (CTEM) : 86,84 % → 94,80 % (+7,96 pts) 📉 WER VoiceCodeBench : 2,3748 % → 1,6107 % (réduction relative de 32,2 %) 🔧 139 erreurs corrigées, 21 succès antérieurs régressés : net +118 entités exactes récupérées Et les gains ont évolué proportionnellement à la quantité de données : 1h : 88,06% CTEM / 59,33% TSR / 2,8188% VCB WER 25h : 92,85% / 72,67% / 1,8517% 100h : 94,80% / 79,00% / 1,6107% Le modèle de 100 heures a récupéré des valeurs que le modèle de base avait manquées : •--revert-last, au lieu de diviser un drapeau en « --revert --last » • tests/auth/login.spec.ts, au lieu de test/auth/login.spec.ts • ALLOWLIST_CIDR, au lieu d'insérer un tiret bas supplémentaire • SN-7KX-9042, au lieu de supprimer le dernier chiffre Les plus grands gains par type d'entité ont été les adresses e-mail (+30,8 pts), les adresses postales (+30,0), les chemins de fichiers (+23,5), les variables d'environnement (+22,9) et les adresses IP (+20,0). outils.text_fr: MiMo-V2.6 est "simplement" le meilleur (pour l'instant). Malgré la simplicité de la conception de son architecture, il est actuellement n°1 des benchmarks de modèles "open-weight" (moyenne pondérée). Par "simple", j'entends une "Grouped Query Attention" (GQA) classique avec une "Sliding Window Attention" (SWA) avec une petite fenêtre de 128 tokens. Cela souligne donc l'un des points que j'ai essayé de faire valoir ces derniers mois : la plupart des progrès proviennent encore des améliorations des données et de la recette de post-entraînement. Les variantes d'attention sophistiquées ne sont pour la plupart que des ajustements d'efficacité. Quelles sont les améliorations des données d'entraînement et de la recette ? L'équipe MiMo a partagé un rapport technique assez détaillé. Il y a beaucoup à digérer, mais en bref, quelques points se sont démarqués : 1. Une augmentation des tâches d'agent ; également un entraînement sur différents "harnesses" (la précision moyenne DeepSWE pass@1 sur les "harnesses" mis de côté est passée d'environ 50 % à 66 %). 2. De meilleurs signaux de récompense : ils ont remplacé un simple vérificateur de justesse par un évaluateur agentique qui examine également les traces d'exécution. 3. De grands lots de RL (1 568 prompts × 16 "rollouts" = 25 088 trajectoires) et 2,7 à 3,7 milliards de "tokens" d'entraînement par mise à jour (mais on ne sait pas ce qu'utilisait le prédécesseur). Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) MiMo-V2.6-Pro fait ses débuts comme le meilleur modèle à poids ouverts sur l'Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (46). À 0,13 $ par tâche de l'Intelligence Index, il se situe sur la frontière de Pareto de l'Intelligence vs. Coût par tâche. @Xiaomi vient de lancer MiMo-V2.6-Pro, un modèle à poids ouverts avec des avancées majeures en intelligence par rapport à son prédécesseur, MiMo-V2.5-Pro (Intelligence Index : 26). Malgré l'amélioration, il conserve le même prix attractif de 0,435 $ par million de "tokens" d'entrée (avec une réduction de 99 % en cas de "cache-hit") et 0,87 $ par million de "tokens" de sortie. Cela fait de MiMo-V2.6-Pro l'un des modèles les plus rentables à déployer. MiMo-V2.6-Pro est un modèle MoE avec 1,02 T de paramètres totaux et 42 milliards de paramètres actifs. outils.text_original: MiMo-V2.6 is "simply" the best (for now). Despite its simple architecture design it's currently No.1 in the open-weight benchmarks (weighted average). With "simple," I mean a classic Grouped Query Attention (GQA) with Sliding Window Attention (SWA) at a tiny 128-token window size. So, that underlines one of the points I've been trying to make in recent months: most of the progress still comes from the data and post-training recipe improvements. Fancy attention variants are just mostly efficiency tweaks. What are some of the training data improvements and recipe improvements? The MiMo team shared a pretty detailed technical report. Lots to carefully digest there, but in short, there are a few things that stood out: 1. An increase in agent tasks; also training across different harnesses (the average DeepSWE pass@1 accuracy on held-out harnesses improved from approximately 50% -> 66%). 2. Better reward signals: they replaced a simple correctness verifier with an agentic grader that looks at the execution traces as well. 3. Large RL batches (1,568 prompts × 16 rollouts = 25,088 trajectories) and 2.7–3.7 billion training tokens per update (unclear, though, what the predecessor used). Despite the improvement, it retains the same attractive pricing at $0.435 per 1M input tokens (with a 99% cache-hit discount) and $0.87 per 1M output tokens. outils.decryptage: "Grouped Query Attention (GQA)" et "Sliding Window Attention (SWA)" sont des techniques d'attention pour les modèles d'IA. Un "token" est une petite unité de texte. Un "MoE model" (Mixture of Experts) combine plusieurs experts pour une tâche. Les "paramètres" sont les valeurs internes d'un modèle ajustées pendant l'entraînement.
